question: A 29-year-old woman, obese, with no history of interest, who consulted for a bilateral, intense, pulsatile headache lasting one month, accompanied by horizontal diplopia and episodes of monocular amaurosis of seconds duration. The exploration is normal, except for the presence of bilateral papilledema. Which of these tests do you think will allow you to fully confirm your diagnosis ?:
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Bilateral papilledema" -> "possible increased intracranial pressure" -> "headache and diplopia symptoms" -> "Magnetic resonance of the skull can identify structural causes" -> "MRI can reveal lesions or abnormalities" -> "confirm diagnosis of intracranial pathology" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Bilateral papilledema" -> "suggests potential neurological issue" -> "headache and visual disturbances present" -> "Lumbar puncture can assess cerebrospinal fluid" -> "CSF analysis may reveal increased pressure or abnormalities" -> "support diagnosis of intracranial hypertension" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Bilateral papilledema" -> "indicates possible intracranial pathology" -> "headache and diplopia symptoms" -> "Electroencephalogram assesses electrical activity" -> "EEG may not directly identify structural issues" -> "less likely to confirm diagnosis" -> 60%

enhanced_information: The presence of bilateral papilledema suggests increased intracranial pressure, which can be associated with various intracranial pathologies. The most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis in this case is a Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the skull, as it can identify structural abnormalities such as tumors, lesions, or other causes of increased intracranial pressure. While a lumbar puncture can assess cerebrospinal fluid and may indicate increased pressure, it is not the primary diagnostic tool for identifying structural causes. An electroencephalogram (EEG) is less relevant for structural diagnosis, and ultrasound of the supra-aortic trunks does not directly address intracranial issues. Visual evoked potentials assess visual pathway function but do not confirm intracranial pathology. Therefore, the MRI is the most definitive test to confirm the diagnosis.
analysis: The clinical presentation of the patient includes bilateral intense pulsatile headaches, horizontal diplopia, episodes of monocular amaurosis, and bilateral papilledema, all of which suggest increased intracranial pressure and potential intracranial pathology. The most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis is a Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the skull, as it can visualize structural abnormalities such as tumors, lesions, or other causes of increased intracranial pressure. While a lumbar puncture can provide information about cerebrospinal fluid and confirm elevated pressure, it does not directly identify the underlying cause. Other options like an electroencephalogram, ultrasound of the supra-aortic trunks, and visual evoked potentials are less relevant for diagnosing structural intracranial issues. Therefore, MRI is the best-supported option for confirming the diagnosis in this case.
